name: Leo M. Suppliers
headline: From an empty shop to everyday responsibility.
intro: Before I built software around everyday operations, I ran them. Leo M. Suppliers started as a field-based fleece-blanket business in February 2022 and became a shop on John Hunt Way in Livingstone. I sold, ordered stock, arranged the displays, carried deliveries out and learned furniture assembly as the range changed. Operations closed in April 2026.
summary: Leo M. Suppliers began with field sales in February 2022 and grew into a physical store in Livingstone. I handled customer relationships, stock decisions, marketing and deliveries, and learned furniture assembly as the business evolved. Operations closed in April 2026, and the experience remains part of how I approach practical problems and the people affected by them.

hero.caption: Inside the shop during its operating years.

photoNote: The photographs come from the shop’s working years and are not dated. The milestones below use the dates I can stand behind, and the chapters describe the shop rather than a dated sequence.

milestones.text: Started selling fleece blankets in the field. The blankets were sourced from Botswana with help from my father, and my mother and sister supported field sales.
Opened a shop at Plot 98, John Hunt Way, Livingstone. The window sign carries the shop’s own numbering, Shop No. 3, alongside the street address.
The range moved from clothing and bedding toward furniture. The change was gradual, and both kinds of stock shared the floor for a while.

chapters.label: 01 / Setting up the shop
chapters.title: Containers, shelving and a floor to fill.
body: Setting up meant packaging and shelving before it meant selling. Furniture arrived flat-packed, so part of the job was opening each box, checking what was inside and putting the pieces together before anything could go on display.
I learned the room as I went: which corner suited the taller pieces, how much space a walkway needs, and what had to sit near the window so people passing on the street could see it.

photos.alt: Cardboard boxes, furniture panels, tools and packaging spread across the shop floor, with clothes hanging on a rail behind
photos.caption: Parts, packaging and tools on the shop floor while furniture was being prepared for display.

chapters.label: 02 / Building the display
chapters.title: Clothing, curtains and household goods, arranged to be found.
body: The shop opened with clothing and bedding. I hung rails along the wall, stacked curtains and blankets where customers could handle them, and kept the smaller household goods within reach near the front.
What people picked up changed the layout. Anything a customer turned over and put back told me how to explain it better the next time, and where it should sit.

photos.caption: Shirts, dresses, curtain rolls and kitchen racks along the back wall.

photos.caption: Cabinets, glass-top stands, textiles and clothing sharing one floor as the range widened.

chapters.label: 03 / The furniture chapter
chapters.title: A harder product to sell, and a better one to learn from.
body: Furniture changed the work. A blanket is easy to compare; a dining set is not. I had to learn the differences between pieces, what each one was made of, and how to talk about size and finish to someone standing in the room.

Assembly became part of the job. Glass tops, pedestal bases, TV brackets and drawer runners all had to be checked before a customer took anything away, because one missing screw turns a sale into a second trip.

chapters.label: 04 / Person and place
chapters.title: The shop was one person answering the questions.
body: I opened up, priced the stock, answered the same questions about price and delivery, carried goods out to customers and locked the door at the end of the day. The photographs with me in them are the honest version of that: one person, a room full of stock and someone waiting for a straight answer.

responsibilities.title: Sourcing and ordering
responsibilities.text: Blankets came from Botswana at the start. Later orders were chosen around what customers kept asking for and what was already moving.

responsibilities.title: Stock decisions
responsibilities.text: Which pieces to hold, what to reorder and what had sat too long. The floor was the record of those decisions.

responsibilities.title: Displays
responsibilities.text: Arranging the shop so a customer could see the range, compare pieces and find the cheaper option without asking.

responsibilities.title: Sales and customers
responsibilities.text: Explaining materials, sizes and finishes, agreeing a price and following up when someone said they would come back.

responsibilities.title: Assembly
responsibilities.text: Learning flat-pack construction as the range changed, and checking every piece before it left the shop.

responsibilities.title: Deliveries and records
responsibilities.text: Taking goods to customers, keeping the paperwork straight and handling the day-to-day running of a registered business.

reading.title: What the photographs show
body: They show the shop’s stock, how it was arranged and the person running it. They do not measure sales, revenue, profit or customer numbers, and neither does this page.
The uploads arrived with messaging-app timestamps, which say nothing about when the shop was photographed. That is why the chapters carry labels instead of dates.

reflection.title: What I took from it
body: Running the shop is where I learned that a system is only as good as its state. A stock count that is wrong once costs a customer, and a payment record that is wrong once costs trust. That is the problem I keep solving in software: what is true, when, and for whom.

Talking to customers every day taught me to explain before persuading. Half of the job was translating what a piece is made of, what fits a small room and why the cheaper option might not last. I write documentation and interface copy with that in mind.
The shop closed in April 2026. What stayed is the habit of checking the details a customer will notice and the ones a system quietly depends on.
